title: How Should I Save for Short-Term vs. Long-Term Goals?
summary: You need separate strategies for your long-term, near-term, and short-term savings. Here's what you need to know.

## **Summary**


- Consider keeping your short-term savings in a high-yield savings or cash management account with low fees, FDIC insurance, and a high Annual Percentage Yield (APY). That way, your money will grow a little and be there when you need it.
- Consider keeping your near-term savings in a high-yield, diversified bond portfolio. That way, your money can grow at a 1–3% higher rate than a high yield cash account with only a minor increase in risk.
- Consider keeping your long-term savings in a low-fee, diversified investment account. That way, your money will have a better shot at keeping up with inflation and increasing your buying power.


No matter what kind of goal you’re saving for, Wealthfront offers the accounts you need to meet them with confidence.


## **How should you categorize short-term, near-term, and long-term** goals?


When you think about your financial future, you probably have three kinds of goals:


- **Short-term goals:** Like a vacation you plan to take later this year
- **Near-term goals:** Like a down payment for a house
- **Long-term goals:** Like sending a child to college or retiring


In order to give yourself the best chance of comfortably reaching those goals, you should approach your short-term, near-term, and long-term savings differently.


### What is the 1–3 and 3–5 year rule?


Knowing when you need your money can help you decide how to save and invest. We like to think of the next five years in three sections. As a rule of thumb, this is the short term, near term, and long term.


**Type of goal** **Time horizon** **Suggested approach**


Short-term Anything in the next year Consider saving cash in a high-yield savings or cash management account


Near-term Something in the next one to three years Consider cash, bonds, a certificate of deposit (CD), or a diversified portfolio of bonds or bond ETFs


Long-term Anything more than three to five years away Consider investing in equities through a diversified investment account


If your goal is in the middle of that range, say four years, you should take into account how flexible your timing is. For example, if you know you will definitely want to buy a new home in four years and you have no flexibility on the timing, you may want to treat that as a near-term goal. But if you are pretty flexible and would be OK waiting another year or so if you needed to, it’s probably fine to treat buying that home as a long-term goal.


**Where should you save for a short-term goal?**


If you have a short-term goal, it’s important to make sure the money you’ll need is available to you in the next year, when you’re ready to invest or spend it. That’s why you should consider saving for short-term goals in a cash management or high-yield savings account (HYSA).


By using a cash management account like the[Wealthfront Cash Account](https://www.wealthfront.com/cash) , you can:


- Avoid taking market risk with your short-term cash
- Earn many times the interest you’d earn at a bank
- Keep your money available when you need it


You should choose an account that doesn’t charge fees, as[fees will erode your wealth over time](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/what-you-should-know-about-bank-fees/) . You’ll also want to pick an account where your savings will be[FDIC insured](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/the-difference-between-fdic-and-sipc-insurance/) . (You can earn an industry-leading APY on your short-term cash with[a Wealthfront Cash Account](https://www.wealthfront.com/start/account-type/for?highLevel=banking&intent=cash&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=pcallout&utm_campaign=shortvslongterm) .)


Earn an industry-leading APY on your short-term cash.[Open a Cash Account](https://www.wealthfront.com/start/account-type/for?highLevel=banking&intent=cash&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=pcallout&utm_campaign=shortvslongterm)


**Should you invest money you need within the next year?**


Avoid the temptation to invest your short-term savings. Financial markets are unpredictable in the short term, and it would be unfortunate to need cash at the exact moment your investment portfolio temporarily declined in value. This is the same reason that it typically makes sense to keep your[emergency fund](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/build-emergency-fund/) in a cash management or high-yield savings account instead of in the market.


## **How should you save or invest for a near-term goal?**


If you’re planning for a big expense in the next three years, we consider that a near-term goal. To save up, you have a few different options.


One option is to hold your savings in your high yield savings or cash account for a longer period of time.


If you’re in the market to buy a home and waiting for the perfect opportunity to come along, you might prefer to hold those savings in cash so that you can jump at the opportunity sooner than you expect.


**When should you consider bonds or a CD?**


If you’re open to taking on some risk and you know the opportunity is going to be at least a year from now, a good option for your savings is to invest in bonds or a certificate of deposit (CD). A CD is a savings account, typically offered by an FDIC-insured bank, where you agree to leave a fixed amount of money untouched for a set period of time in exchange for a higher interest rate.


Fixed income products like bonds and CDs are lower risk than equities but have a higher potential earning than saving your money in cash. It can be tempting to put all of your extra cash in just one or two bonds, but like investing in equities, one of the best ways to mitigate risk is to diversify across multiple bonds or bond ETFs.


**How can you invest in bonds?**


There are many ways to invest in bonds:


- Purchase a bond directly through a brokerage firm
- Purchase a Treasury bond through TreasuryDirect
- Invest in bond ETFs
- Invest in bond mutual funds


Unfortunately, buying bonds directly can come with challenges:


- High minimums
- Lack of diversification
- Liquidity restrictions


**How do bond ETFs differ from individual bonds and CDs?**


Bond ETFs can help address these obstacles because, like stock ETFs, they trade on stock exchanges throughout the trading day and typically hold a diversified portfolio of bonds. This structure can provide investors with greater liquidity than purchasing certain individual bonds directly. This means:


- The money is available to you regardless of a single bond’s maturity date
- Bond ETFs are naturally more diversified than an individual bond


**How does Wealthfront’s Automated Bond Portfolio work?**


Our[Automated Bond Portfolio](https://www.wealthfront.com/automated-bond-portfolio) is made of a diversified mix of bond ETFs designed to provide a higher yield than Treasury bills, CDs, and high-yield savings accounts. It provides:


- More liquidity than bonds and CDs
- Less risk than equities and corporate bonds
- Tax optimization for your personal situation


This combination makes it a great place to grow the savings that you need soon, but not urgently.


## **How should you save for a long-term goal?**


If you’re saving for a purchase you won’t make within the next three to five years, that’s a long-term goal. To save for your long-term goals, a good option is to invest in equities.


**Why might cash or bonds be unsuitable for long-term goals?**


Many people are tempted to hold their long-term savings in cash. But the[problem with saving for long-term goals in a savings or cash account](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/your-high-yield-cash-account-shouldnt-be-your-only-savings-vehicle/) —even a high-yield account—or[in bonds](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/invest-when-rates-rise/) is that the rate of earning on these accounts has seldom kept up with[inflation](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/the-right-and-wrong-ways-to-protect-yourself-from-inflation/) over the last decade.


This means over time your savings can actually lose buying power. Investing in equities can help you avoid this problem by allowing you to earn a higher rate of return over the long term with added risk.


**How should you plan to invest for a long-term goal?**


There are endless ways you can invest your money, but we suggest investing in a[diversified](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/what-is-diversification/) portfolio of low-cost index funds instead of investing your life’s savings in individual stocks, which is riskier and more likely to underperform the market’s annualized return.


You don’t have to take our word for it:[academic research](https://finance.martinsewell.com/capm/Markowitz1952.pdf) has consistently found that diversifying your portfolio across asset classes is one of the best ways to maximize returns across every level of risk.


You can start building long-term wealth with investing best practices with[The Wealthfront Portfolio](https://www.wealthfront.com/investing) .


Wealthfront automates investing best practices to help you build long-term wealth.[Open The Wealthfront Portfolio](https://www.wealthfront.com/start/account-type/goal?intent=investing&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=pcallout&utm_campaign=shortvslongterm)


**Should you use a tax-advantaged or taxable investment account?**


When choosing an investment account, there are two main types to consider:


**Account type** **Features and considerations**


Tax-advantaged Certain tax breaks or tax savings included
May include restrictions or penalties
Examples include: 529 College Savings Account, IRA
Has withdrawal restrictions & early withdrawal penalties
No tax-loss harvesting


Taxable Highly flexible accounts
Use funds for any reason
No withdrawal penalties
Can apply Tax-Loss Harvesting
Has tax implications on dividends, interest payments, and realized capital gains
No upfront tax deduction or tax free growth


**How can tax-loss harvesting help in a taxable account?**


If you use a taxable account, you can help lower your tax bill with[tax-loss harvesting](https://research.wealthfront.com/whitepapers/tax-loss-harvesting/) —a strategy that takes advantage of market volatility. How much can this help? When we use each client’s inferred tax rate to estimate their benefit from Tax-Loss Harvesting and compare that benefit to the actual amount they paid in advisory fees, we find that for nearly[95% of clients](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/tlh-results-2025/) who have used Tax-Loss Harvesting for at least a year in The Wealthfront Portfolio or direct indexing account, the estimated tax benefit exceeds fees paid.


In short, using a taxable investment account to save for a long-term goal means your savings have a better chance of increasing in buying power and growing significantly—and you’ll also have plenty of flexibility.


Typically, the[longer you stay invested](https://www.wealthfront.com/blog/think-long-term-investing/) , the better the odds that you’ll earn returns.


**How are risk, return, and your time horizon connected?**


There’s an easy way to think about saving for your goals: risk and return are correlated. The higher the risk, the higher the expected return. This means:


- In situations where you can’t afford to take any market risk, like saving for a short-term goal, you’ll sacrifice higher returns
- When you have a longer time horizon, your willingness to take on market risk can result in higher returns

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What counts as a short-term financial goal?**


As a rule of thumb, we define a short-term goal as anything in the next year. A vacation you plan to take later this year is one example.


### **What counts as a near-term financial goal?**


We consider a big expense one to three years from now a near-term goal. A down payment for a house is one example.


### **What counts as a long-term financial goal?**


A long-term goal is anything more than three to five years away. Examples include sending a child to college or retiring.


### **Where should I keep my emergency fund?**


It typically makes sense to keep your emergency fund in a high-yield cash account instead of in the market. Financial markets are unpredictable in the short term.


### **Should I treat a goal four years away as near-term or long-term?**


This will depend on your individual situation. You should take into account how flexible your timing is. If you have no flexibility, you may want to treat it as a near-term goal, but if you would be OK waiting another year or so, it’s probably fine to treat it as a long-term goal.


### **Why diversify across multiple bonds or bond ETFs?**


Like investing in equities, one of the best ways to mitigate risk is to diversify across multiple bonds or bond ETFs. Bond ETFs hold a basket of bonds, making them naturally more diversified than an individual bond.


### **What is the difference between a taxable and tax-advantaged account?**


Tax-advantaged accounts come with tax breaks but also have withdrawal restrictions and penalties if you don’t use them according to the rules governing each specific account type. Taxable accounts are highly flexible, can be used for whatever you want, and don’t charge a withdrawal penalty for taking your money out. However, you may owe taxes on realized investment gains, dividends, and interest.


### **Why invest long-term savings instead of holding them in cash?**


The rate of earning on savings or cash accounts, even high-yield ones, or even in bonds has seldom kept up with inflation over the last decade. Investing in equities can help you avoid losing buying power by allowing you to earn a higher rate of return over the long term with added risk.
